articles.title_orig: Trump administration weighs new penalties against China over jailed Americans - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Trump administration weighs new penalties against China over jailed Americans - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Beijing has shut down attempts to open negotiations, officials say.
As President Donald Trump makes a high-stakes visit to China, U.S. officials told ABC News his administration is evaluating options aimed at pressuring Beijing to free two American citizens wrongfully detained in the country on allegations of espionage.
Trump has raised the cases of Youlin Chen, a Boston-based seismologist, and Min Zin, a doctoral candidate at University of California, Berkeley, in previous engagements with China’s President Xi Jinping, but the Chinese government has not seriously engaged in any negotiations for their release, according to the officials.
A likely next move would be elevating the State Department’s travel advisory level for China, a diplomatic consequence that can have chilling effect on travel and tourism, U.S. officials told ABC News.
A significantly more severe penalty would be designating China as a State Sponsor of Wrongful Detention , a measure that opens up a range of punitive measures the U.S. government can opt to employ, including financial sanctions and visa restrictions. The officials did not indicate the administration was ready to take that step yet, but said the option remains on the table.
The officials also said the administration would likely wait to take any action until sometime after the president returns from Asia, in order to give talks space to progress.
“We do not preview potential designations or changes to travel advisories,” a State Department spokesman said. “We will continue to evaluate the risks facing Americans in China and take appropriate steps to protect U.S. citizens.”
The president indicated earlier this month he intended to talk to Xi about Americans detained in China during their meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen, China on Thursday.
“I do talk to him about that a lot. And we've done well,” Trump told reporters on Nov. 6 in West Palm Beach, Florida.
The State Department added a wrongful detention risk indicator to its travel advisory for mainland China in October, a move one official said was intended to both alert Americans to potential danger and warn Beijing that additional repercussions were on the horizon.
China’s foreign ministry has repeatedly rejected the State Department’s determination that Chen and Zin and wrongfully detained and maintains that Chinese judicial authorities are handling the cases in accordance with the country’s laws.
Under China’s sweeping national security laws, routine research and data collection may be interpreted as a threat to the country’s interests – putting academics at greater risk of wrongful detention, according to the State Department.
Critics of the Chinese government also say that its national security laws enable the Chinese Communist Party to target foreign nationals involved with topics it deems politically sensitive.
The policy is seemingly at odds with Beijing’s push to expand tourism and academic exchanges with foreign institutions, including those in the U.S. Following a visit to Washington in September , Xi announced a new initiative to invite 100,000 young Americans to study in China over five years.
The U.S. government has determined that the allegations against both Chen and Zin are meritless and classified both men as wrongfully detained.
Chen was detained in 2024 by state security agents during a trip to visit family members in China. Authorities charged him with espionage and are currently holding him in pre-trial detention.
Zin traveled to China to attend an academic conference at Beijing’s invitation in June. Upon his arrival, he was arrested on suspicion of engaging in espionage. He has not yet been formally charged.
While Chen and Zin are the only Americans officially labeled as wrongfully detained by the Chinese government, experts estimate that dozens of Americans in China are subject to exit bans or other coercive measures that limit their ability to leave the country.
Trump is expected to meet face-to-face with Xi at least one more time this year when G20 leaders gather in Miami for the group’s annual summit in December.
“I’ve been assured that President Trump remains firmly committed to securing Youlin’s freedom and that he intends to raise Youlin’s case with President Xi at both the APEC meeting and, if needed, the G20,” Chen’s wife, Yufang Chen, said in a statement to ABC News.
“We all know that when President Trump gets involved, Americans come home,” she added.
Sylvia Zin, Min Zin’s wife, told ABC News she recently learned her husband was hospitalized last month for severe dehydration and that there is no heat at the location where he is being held.
"My worry for my husband's health and wellbeing increases with each passing day,” she said in a statement. "My daughter and I remain hopeful in the President's ability to bring him home to us in time for the holidays."
An ABC News request to the Chinese Embassy for comment on Zin’s status and medical condition did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Gulf states and tankers under fire as U.S. and Iran ramp back up tit-for-tat strikes
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Gulf states and tankers under fire as U.S. and Iran ramp back up tit-for-tat strikes
articles.content_orig:
Iran has launched new attacks on its Gulf neighbours, targeting an airbase used by the United States military in Kuwait and carrying out several attacks on Bahrain after the US bombed Iran’s Qeshm Island.
Kuwait said it activated its air defences to counter drone strikes – the first since early September – and Bahrain said it fended off an Iranian attack early on Wednesday, a day after the US attacked a missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
The US said it carried out the strike in response to an Iranian attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain earlier on Tuesday.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s 5th Fleet, has experienced four Iranian attacks in six days, ending a weeks-long respite in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
Iran said its recent attacks were in response to US drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.
The uptick in fighting raises the risk of a wider escalation towards the resumption of all-out conflict nearly nine months into the war, and complicates negotiations for a diplomatic solution, which have stagnated despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
The Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries have drawn condemnation from across the region.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Iranian attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain “in the strongest terms” and denounced an attack on a tanker belonging to the United Arab Emirates.
The ministry said the kingdom rejects Iran’s disruption of shipping routes and urged a negotiated solution.
Arab League chief Nabil Fahmy said the repeated attacks on Arab countries reveal “a continuous escalation pattern that threatens to widen the circle of confrontation”. He also condemned the targeting of a ship belonging to the UAE’s national oil company, ADNOC, as it crossed the Strait of Hormuz.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, the Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, held Iran “responsible for this escalation and its repercussions on regional security”.
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry called the attacks “a dangerous escalation” that risks undermining diplomatic efforts. Kuwait and the UAE also condemned them.
Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry described the drone attacks as flagrant violations of its sovereignty and a direct threat to its security, Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi reported from Doha.
Basravi also said Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed al-Ansari, warned that continued escalation without restraint from both the US and Iran makes a negotiated solution, or even continued dialogue, harder.
Meanwhile, Iran’s army chief, Major-General Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were “monitoring the enemy’s movements” after a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East, the Fars news agency reported.
He said Iran’s response to any misstep by the US and its “backers” would be “even more crushing”.

articles.title_orig: China watchdog warns Trump faces ‘2-on-1’ showdown with Xi, Putin as Taiwan risks mount
articles.title_zh: China watchdog warns Trump faces ‘2-on-1’ showdown with Xi, Putin as Taiwan risks mount
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.
President Donald Trump meets with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel, on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Responding to concerns about Taiwan , a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.
"Under President Trump’s leadership, U.S.-China relations have been refocused on what matters most – rebuilding the safety, security and prosperity of Americans. And as President Trump has said: much has been, and will be, accomplished, between the two leaders," the official said.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the President of the United States, the President of the People’s Republic of China, and the President of the Russian Federation."
"The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," the official added.
TRUMP’S TAIWAN ‘NEGOTIATING CHIP’ REMARK SPARKS ALARM OVER HOW FAR HE'D SHIFT US-CHINA POLICY
A procession of Taiwanese armed military vehicles patrols outside the Songshan Airport in the capital city following China’s announcement of the military exercise Joint Sword-2024B that encircles Taiwan, Oct. 14, 2024, in Taipei, Taiwan. (Daniel

articles.title_orig: Israeli Tanks Advance Across Gaza Cease-Fire Line in Rare Incursion
articles.title_zh: Israeli Tanks Advance Across Gaza Cease-Fire Line in Rare Incursion
articles.content_orig:
Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order
Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.
Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.
It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.
Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Israel building new land barriers in Gaza and displacing families
Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The Israeli military said the first two strikes targeted "terrorists" and that it was not aware of the third incident, according to AFP news agency.
At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title_orig: PlayStation suffers major outage hours before "GTA VI" launch
articles.title_zh: PlayStation suffers major outage hours before "GTA VI" launch
articles.content_orig:
Disruption comes at critical moment, with Grand Theft Auto VI one of the most eagerly anticipated titles in history
PlayStation has suffered widespread network problems just hours before the release of Grand Theft Auto VI , one of the most eagerly anticipated titles in recent gaming history.
The disruption emerged Wednesday, causing frustrated players to flood social media with complaints about failed logins and server connection problems downloading games and updates.
PlayStation’s official network status page acknowledged problems affecting its gaming and social services, which has left players struggling to access online features.
“You might have difficulty launching games, apps, or network features. We’re working to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Thank you for your patience,” the alert read.
Many affected users said their internet connections were working normally, suggesting the problems were specifically affecting PlayStation’s online services. Some PS5 owners said that their consoles successfully completed internet connection tests, only for the “Sign in to online services” check to fail.
The scale of the disruption was reflected on Downdetector , a website that tracks real-time service outages, which cited 1,228 user reports of PlayStation outages by Wednesday afternoon.
The website monitors disruptions using reports submitted by users, with sudden spikes potentially indicating that large numbers of people are experiencing similar technical difficulties. The reports do not independently confirm the extent of an official outage, however.
Although no official cause has been established, the timing of the problems has raised questions about whether the issue could be linked to a recently released PS5 software update. Sony announced Tuesday evening that it had rolled out a system software update required for users planning to play GTA VI.
Sony’s official troubleshooting advice recommends that affected players examine their system software and internet connections.
The disruption comes at a critical moment for PlayStation users, with GTA VI scheduled to launch at midnight Thursday.
GTA VI is being lauded as the most anticipated game in history. The hype for the latest installment of the iconic GTA franchise, the first new game in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has already suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game.

articles.title_orig: Trump and Xi are set to meet in China amid tensions over AI. Here's what to know.
articles.title_zh: Trump and Xi are set to meet in China amid tensions over AI. Here's what to know.
articles.content_orig:
Washington — President Trump is holding a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, against the backdrop of a widening scandal over advanced U.S. chips reaching China and internal divisions within Mr. Trump's Cabinet about how to address it.
The bilateral meeting is taking place in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, known as APEC. Mr. Trump embraced Xi when he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday.
It's the third time the two world leaders are meeting face to face this year. The last time they met was in September, when Mr. Trump hosted Xi for a three-day summit at the White House. Mr. Trump is hosting Xi again for the G20 Leaders' Summit at Trump National Doral in Miami in December.
The Trump-Xi meeting will be followed by a meeting of Mr. Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Here's what Mr. Trump and Xi are likely to discuss.
Mr. Trump told reporters as he left for Asia that he may bring up Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The Justice Department has been investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed for diverting semiconductor chips to China.
The president has cast doubts on assessments that Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset.
"I don't know that she is a spy," he said. "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country, that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the scandal is much bigger than Jensen Huang and his alleged affairs.
"It's really kind of unfolded into a much bigger, longer-term scandal that involves the question of how many chips did China get, how porous were export controls, and how did the Commerce Department enforce them?" McGuire said on a phone briefing with reporters Wednesday. "Which I think is a much more important, longer-term strategic question for the United States, for the U.S.-China relationship than anything involving Jensen Huang's personal affairs."
Shortly before the president left for Asia, the Trump administration announced new interim trade rules that will restrict Chinese AI companies from accessing advanced U.S. chips remotely.
The move comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of slow-walking restrictions on Megaspeed, revealing a rift between Bessent and Lutnick. Bessent told CNBC that Mr. Trump had indicated that China should not have access to the chips, but suggested that Lutnick was resisting. The president didn't take sides in the Bessent-Lutnick debate, telling reporters before he left for Asia that the men have "two different views" where "one wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China."
"One view is you don't want to insult China," Mr. Trump said Monday. "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them. And the other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do. Both can say either is wrong or right."
Ultimately, the Treasury Department and National Security Council, not the Commerce Department under Lutnick, wrote  the new interim rule cutting off Chinese companies from remotely accessing the most advanced AI chips in data centers abroad, though the Commerce Department issued the rule.
"This is a very significant action that really cuts off a lot of the avenues that China is using to get AI computing power," McGuire said. "There was a digital forensic study that was done recently that showed that every single advanced Chinese model is actually trained with the most advanced American chips, so even though these chips have been banned to China, the controls have not been effective. They've probably had some impact but not that much."
The actions taken on Monday, however, will have a "really significant" effect on China's access to computing power, which "could materially widen the lead" between the U.S. and China on AI, McGuire said.
Mr. Trump has shown no signs of wanting to slow the United States' AI advancement in the race against China. After a September summit between Mr. Trump and Xi, the U.S. and Chinese governments pledged to set up a communication channel to share information when AI goes off the rails.
But talking about wayward AI incidents after the fact isn't nearly enough, said Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow on technology with the Asia Society Policy Institute and a digital fellow with the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.
Graylin will be interested to see if Mr. Trump and Xi can work past the negative news cycle, like the Jensen Huang scandal, to take more steps on AI safety collaboration by bringing together more technical experts for working-level discussions.
"I hope that we go beyond just having surface level discussion, and we start to actually create some enduring institutions around safety," Graylin said.
Before leaving for Asia, Mr. Trump was asked if he'll bring up Taiwan in his meeting with Xi.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," the president responded. "I won't have to raise it."
David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations — not the former White House AI czar David Sacks — said he thinks that's right.
"I think that it's very clear that every time Xi sees Trump, they do a little check-in on Taiwan, and Xi Jinping raises his concerns on Taiwan and his expectations of how President Trump will handle Taiwan and cross-strait dynamics," Sacks told reporters on the Council on Foreign Relations call.
A $14 billion arms package to Taiwan is still pending on the president's desk, Sacks said. Earlier this year, the Navy said the arms sale had been put on "pause" to make sure the U.S. military had enough munitions for the Iran war. Sacks said there will be "more pressure from Congress in the coming months to move that arms package forward."
"And so, if President Trump is determined to resist that, you know he will need, you know — Xi Jinping will hope to kind of stiffen his spine and say, 'You're on the right track, and if you approve this arms package, you're going to send cross-strait relations reeling.'"
Lyle Goldstein, the director of Defense Priorities Asia, told CBS News he is actually optimistic about a Trump-Putin-Xi meeting. Goldstein said he doesn't think any "major results" will come out of the sit-down, but the discussions might bear fruit in a future U.S.-China-Russia meeting.
"I actually think it could allow for some, not for breakthroughs, but for some movement on major issues," Goldstein said. "And this is the first time ever that you have this trilateral format for Russia, China, and the U.S. So I would like to see this continue."
Mr. Trump said he has a range of topics to discuss with both Xi and Putin when they meet, including denuclearization.
"We're going to talk about denuclearization," Mr. Trump said. "Tough subject, because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right? Especially since you do have other countries."
They'll also discuss Iran, the U.S. president said. On Tuesday, Mr. Trump said Iran would have a major price to pay if it detonates a so-called dirty bomb, after CNN reported U.S. intelligence indicates Iran may be developing plans to set off such a device in the nation's capital.
The White House previously said Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion in the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting, since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said Ukraine will be a topic for the three leaders.
"We'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine," he told reporters.

articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Falls as Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors' Nerves
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares declined another 2.89% Wednesday after the company issued its first earnings report since the departure of former CEO Jensen Huang . The stock is down more than 13% over the past week.
Trading in the neocloud companies was volatile throughout the day, as CoreWeave closed down 4.13%, Iren sank 3.61% and Nebius whipsawed, ending the trading day up 0.87%.
Nvidia's third-quarter revenue came in at $115.84 billion, more than $6 billion above analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion topped the $125.1 billion consensus, according to LSEG.
The semiconductor giant continues to navigate the fallout from Huang's resignation last week. Shortly before the results, Huang made his first public statement since resigning last week, saying that he was open to returning to the company, after an outpouring of support from prominent tech figures .
But Harvey Jones, the new and first-ever chair of Nvidia's board, said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO.
″[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," interim CEO Colette Kress told Jim Cramer on CNBC's "Mad Money."
"This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers — that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breath of different customers."
The U.S. Commerce Department announced a legal change on Monday to try and stem China's access to the most advanced Nvidia chips — which are already under export controls effectively preventing their import into the country — by restricting Chinese companies' ability to access compute remotely in overseas data centers.
In a letter Wednesday, the House Energy and Commerce Committee asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear to discuss chip export controls, and requested a briefing from interim CEO Colette Kress by Dec. 2.
Nvidia told investors in its earnings commentary that it was "not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook," in keeping with its recent language on the country.
Huang is slated to appear before several Congressional committees in the coming weeks.
Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday, Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Huang and Lutnick have agreed to appear before the committee in December. articles.title_orig: Britain, EU drop 'trusted partnership' term from summit draft
articles.title_zh: Britain, EU drop 'trusted partnership' term from summit draft
articles.content_orig:
Leaked text of 72-paragraph second draft shows agreement has largely been reached before expected signoff on Friday
The UK-EU “relationship reset” agreement, which began in earnest under Keir Starmer, is expected to be signed off by Andy Burnham in Brussels on Friday.
A leaked text of the second draft shows an agreement has largely been reached with some outstanding points.
Here’s what is and isn’t addressed in the 72-paragraph joint communique, from pet passports and cheese imports to student fees and artist touring visas.
You may not make it. The deal states it will “allow people from the EU and the UK to reside for up to three years to engage in activities such as work, studies, au pairing, volunteering, or simply travelling”.
But the deal may not be active until 2030 because work permits are the preserve of national governments, not something Brussels can solve.
“We aim to apply this agreement no later than 2028 and endeavour to ensure that opportunities under the scheme will be available to our young people no later than January 2030,” the draft says.
This has yet to be agreed. The two options in the draft text are a halfway house between international and home fees, or a concession from the UK to allow EU citizens pay the same as British students (or Irish ones, who are also eligible for home fees under a separate longstanding agreement).
The choices, according to the draft, are “significantly reduced undergraduate” or “equal treatment” with UK nationals on tuition fees.
The British government wants to cap youth mobility at between 50,000 and 80,000 places to reduce impact on overall migration numbers. The EU is pushing for at least 100,000.
Some EU states, including Germany, are open to the idea of allowing unlimited numbers of British young people to work, live or study in their countries regardless of UK reciprocation.
Elton John has long been among those demanding the government fix a flaw in the Brexit deal which saw gigging bands or theatre groups unable to tour Europe without major bureaucracy (and its associated cost) since 2021.
The EU has resisted negotiating on the issue because, like youth mobility, it touches on work permits which are a national remit. But in what appears to be a win for the UK, touring artists do feature in the draft text.
No deal been reached, but it has been agreed that “the EU and the UK should explore further mutually beneficial solutions” for “touring artists”.
Not yet. The draft agreement says the sanitary and phyto-sanitary (SPS) agreement will not be implemented until 1 March 2028.
This takes into account primary legislation that is needed on the UK side to dynamically align with EU standards.
No. These are tied to the SPS deal, meaning British travellers will still have to fork out up to £200 every time they take their dog or cat to an EU country.
Travel and transport officials are hoping relevant changes to the SPS agreement can be brought forward.
“Around 15% of our customers have pets with them. For them it will make a huge difference,” Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the owner of Eurotunnel, told the Guardian.
No. The EU has pressed the UK to follow its trade defence measures which include quotas on Chinese hybrid-electric cars and tariffs on fully electric cars.
The UK has said it will not be coerced into a decision but is demanding that British manufacturers are not locked out of the upcoming Made in Europe legislation in exchange for forming a kind of trade club with the EU on autos.
Both sides agree to protectionist measures in “a particular supply chain” but there is no agreement yet on how that will apply. According to the text, the EU proposes that “the UK would be bound to ensure in its policies and national legal order the same outcomes” as measures imposed by the EU. The UK’s proposed text says: “We will aim to protect supply chains consistently across our markets and guard against potential risks of circumvention.”
It’s gone. Instead of a vague “trusted partnership”, both sides commit to a “partnership for economic resilience”.
The language in the latest draft agreement has also been tightened up in a concession to the UK, say diplomats.
The UK wants to restore pre-Brexit access to EU databases but this will not be agreed on Friday. The EU will instead explore giving the UK access to its proposed Prüm International scheme “on data exchange for police cooperation to chosen third-country partners”.
There is no mention of Eurodac, the database that stores biometrics of asylum seekers in the EU, and diplomats say sharing this data, which was not collected for law enforcement purposes, could be tricky.
But according to the draft, the EU will “continue exploring ways to reinforce mutual and reciprocal exchanges of data on criminal records of third-country nationals”.

articles.title_orig: Fed Officials Saw Higher Rates Ahead When They Held Steady Last Month
articles.title_zh: Fed Officials Saw Higher Rates Ahead When They Held Steady Last Month
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday.
Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk."
More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December.
The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."
In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December.
Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability.
Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint."
"Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms."
Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off.
Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase.
Those voting in favor of the hold "pointed to benefits in accumulating additional information, which would help in determining the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
Since the meeting, the inflation data has shown that the pace of price increases remains well above target.
The consumer price index in October rose 0.4% for all items and 0.3% for the core that excludes food and energy. Both readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than expected.
While indicating concern over how stubborn inflation has been, most Fed officials who have spoken publicly advocated a patient approach.
However, Waller said Wednesday that the Fed may have to "shock" markets by approving a half-point hike in December. He is the only central banker to espouse that belief publicly, though St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he anticipates as much as a full percentage point move higher by the spring of 2027. As governor, Waller is a permanent FOMC voter; Musalem will not vote until 2028.
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday on CNBC that the central bank risks losing its credibility if it doesn't act.
At the core of policymakers' concern is whether rising prices related to the Iran war and President Donald Trump 's tariffs, in many cases temporary events that wouldn't prompt a response, are instead becoming more entrenched.
Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting that includes low odds of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Futures traders also are pricing a solid likelihood of two more increases in 2027.

articles.title_orig: Trump is trying to put the Iran war behind him, but it’s not over
articles.title_zh: Trump is trying to put the Iran war behind him, but it’s not over
articles.content_orig:
Tehran, Iran – Iranian forces have targeted military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait as the United States has hit military and radar installations in southern Iran after a spate of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Both the US and Iran appear reluctant for all-out conflict again, as happened during the opening weeks of the war, which the US and Israel began on February 28. But analysts said the current situation is inherently unstable and could potentially escalate again into full-blown war that could see Israel rejoin the strikes on Iran.
US forces are deployed at military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait, which Tehran considers complicit in the recent strikes on southern Iran. The two countries had not been attacked since early September, but both have been targeted by Iranian drones in recent days.
The lull for Bahrain ended on November 13 when Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) directed explosive-laden drones towards the Riffa Air Base after US air strikes in Sirik, a port on Iran’s Hormozgan coast. Several more Iranian strikes have followed, and the US has also attacked Iran’s Qeshm Island on multiple occasions.
After hitting Bahrain, the IRGC warned Manama against its security partnership with the US and its treatment of Shia Muslim leaders after several were recently given lengthy prison sentences.
Kuwait reported incoming drones overnight into Wednesday. Iran’s military said it was targeting US equipment at Ali Al Salem Air Base, including missile launch platforms. No Iranian missiles were used against Bahrain or Kuwait, unlike attacks earlier in the war, according to reports.
Mohammad Eslami, a Tehran-based foreign policy analyst, said Iran aims to gradually degrade US military assets across the region, particularly those Tehran believes were active during the war.
“So long as the war does not end in a political agreement, Iran will continue to do this, regardless of other factors like the blockade,” he told Al Jazeera.
US President Donald Trump and senior officials in his administration have insisted a naval blockade on southern Iranian ports and tough sanctions against Tehran are working. These appear designed to either force Iran to concede to US demands for ending the war or lead to the collapse of its government.
But Tehran is increasingly signalling that it will not accept a continuation of the status quo as the sanctions are severely impacting imports and exports to Iran. The Iranian military’s targeting of regional military facilities this week is likely related to this US economic embargo, said Andreas Krieg, an associate professor in security studies at King’s College London.
“The strikes on Bahrain and Kuwait are about probing American red lines, testing how far Tehran can push the boundaries of military confrontation without triggering another full-scale war,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.
“By targeting American assets in Gulf states, Iran is trying to make Washington’s economic warfare increasingly costly for its regional partners.”
The US military’s Central Command says its maritime blockade has prevented Iran from loading any crude oil onto its tankers since late August. It has also claimed more than 1.7 billion barrels of crude have been shipped through the Strait of Hormuz by Iran’s Arab neighbours under US protection and in defiance of demands for vessels to use a route Tehran has authorised.
Iran continues to sell oil stored outside the blockade limits to China, although at reduced levels.
The IRGC maintains that the strait remains closed to unauthorised transit and continues to target the oil shuttle system, which it believes is run primarily by the United Arab Emirates . This relay system has succeeded in getting more energy exports out of the Gulf using tankers that transfer their cargoes to other ships that deliver the oil to global markets.
The UAE’s state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) confirmed on Wednesday that one of its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz and one crew member was missing.
To reopen the strategic waterway, Tehran has demanded the US lift its blockade and an Iran-Oman deal outlining coordinated transit routes in the strait be honoured along with other carefully sequenced US concessions on lifting the sanctions on Iran and releasing its frozen assets.
Mediators like Qatar and Pakistan continue to try to bridge the gaps between the two sides, but the talks have largely reached an impasse as both sides refuse to budge on their main demands.
Eslami said Trump and his senior political and military officials have failed to adopt a clear strategy towards Tehran, particularly in light of Iran’s promise of a response across the region and beyond if attacked.
“The “Iron Gate” and other measures are effectively a pretty name for their indecision,” he said about the US plan to create overland trade disruptions . “The issue in the negotiations is that they don’t know what to do about the raised proposals due to the political costs they would have to pay in the US.”
Still, some Iranians appear to believe they are the dominant party in the current impasse. Speaking to state television on Wednesday, the IRGC’s political deput,y Yadollah Javani, said Trump was stuck in a “quagmire” and must accept defeat.
“Trump has no choice but to accept realities in the field,” he said, adding that Iran was upgrading its arsenal and prepared for another major outbreak in fighting with the US.
After a third US aircraft carrier strike group entered the Arabian Sea, Iran’s army chief, Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were prepared for any new attacks by Washington.
“The enemy is preparing its forces, but the army and other armed forces monitor their movements vigilantly,” he said in a speech on Wednesday. “The preparedness of armed forces increases by the moment. Our response to any error by the enemy and its backers will be more decisive than before.”
Trump’s administration appears split on how to handle Iran with hawks such as Defense Secretary Pete Hesgeth reportedly wanting a more forceful approach to Tehran.
Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said others believe Washington can maintain the blockade and economic pressure indefinitely while avoiding full-scale war. But the latest attacks demonstrate the difficulty of maintaining such an arrangement.
“Beyond the risk of unintended escalation, the longer the blockade and economic pressure campaigns continue, the greater the incentive for Tehran to deliberately escalate in an attempt to break the deadlock by force,” he wrote in an analysis online.
Krieg said he expects Tehran to intensify calibrated pressure through attacks on US military assets and by continuing to target vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz.
This strategy could also potentially press the Iran-allied Houthis, the Yemeni armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), to make further advances along the Bab al-Mandeb strait , another strategic chokepoint for maritime trade and global energy supplies.
“But this equilibrium is inherently unstable. If diplomacy fails to produce tangible economic relief, I believe further escalation will become increasingly likely,” Krieg said. “The greatest danger is that both sides keep pushing each other’s thresholds until one crosses a red line neither fully understood.”

articles.title_orig: Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit
articles.title_zh: Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit
articles.content_orig:
Humilis Investment Strategies CEO and CIO Brian Belski joins Taylor Riggs to analyze Nvidia's third-quarter earnings beat, showing a 103% year-over-year revenue surge. They also discuss the board's decision regarding Jensen Huang.
Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday's earnings call that the company is well-positioned to move forward following the abrupt resignation of co-founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang last week following the revelation of extramarital affairs.
Kress, who has served as Nvidia's CFO since 2013, delivered the AI giant's first quarterly earnings report since Huang's departure, which beat the market's expectations in terms of revenue and earnings per share.
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this," Kress said on the call.
"With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia's leadership position," she added.
NVIDIA RELEASES QUARTERLY EARNINGS, SUGGESTS FUTURE PLANS AFTER JENSEN HUANG'S RESIGNATION
Nvidia's quarterly earnings beat the market's expectations in its first report since Jensen Huang's resignation. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Investors were looking for the company to provide reassurance about its path forward as well as to post strong results over the prior three months in what was viewed as a test for the durability of the AI trade .
Nvidia's earnings beat analysts' estimates for quarterly revenue , which came in at $115.8 billion and topped the estimate of $109.1 billion reflected in data compiled by LSEG. Diluted earnings per share were $2.68, beating the estimate of $2.48.
Revenue was up 20% on a quarterly basis and 103% year over year, while earnings per share rose 10% from the prior quarter and 108% from a year ago. Nvidia's net income for the quarter was $65.3 billion, which represents a quarterly increase of 9% and a rise of 105% year over year.
Nvidia lifted its forecast for the fourth quarter of its fiscal 2027, which includes an additional week, to project $130 billion in revenue, plus or minus 3%; while Kress said the company raised its fiscal year 2028 outlook with revenue growth of 75% year over year, an increase from 70%.
JENSEN HUANG SAYS HE IS WILLING TO RETURN AS NVIDIA CEO, SAYING 'I OWN MY MISTAKES COMPLETELY'
Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. (Nvidia/Handout)
She also noted that Nvidia's cloud industry backlog grew to $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago, which underscored the "significant multiyear opportunity ahead of our partners and of Nvidia."
Earlier on Tuesday before the earnings release, Huang released a statement saying that "I own my mistakes completely" and that he would be open to returning as the company's CEO if the board of directors thought it would be "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America."
Harvey Jones, chairman of the Nvidia board of directors, shut down that speculation on the earnings call, saying that Huang voluntarily resigned and the board "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
NVIDIA ADDS BOARD OVERSIGHT OF NATIONAL SECURITY AND EXPORT COMPLIANCE
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would be willing to return as CEO after resigning last week, though the board chairman later said directors don't plan to do so. (Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images)

articles.title_zh: Stocks Fall as Nvidia’s Earnings Rally Sputters: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) bulls are getting hit with another reality check in a saga now in its second week.
That is, with no visionary Jensen Huang at the company, Nvidia is, well, just another chip company — one that's searching for somebody to fill a giant black leather jacket in the C-suite.
Shares of the tech giant reversed sharply on Wednesday from an initial positive post-earnings reaction. Nvidia stock is down about 3.5% at the time of this writing, reversing an almost 4% premarket pop.
"We view recently ousted founding CEO Jensen Huang as a singular leader who leaves impossible shoes to fill. Huang's departure creates a leadership vacuum which nature (and investors) abhor(s)," Oppenheimer analyst Rich Schafer said.
Schafer said he still has no price target on Nvidia's stock given the volatility. He removed his price target several days earlier.
Interim CEO Colette Kress made a solid case late Tuesday for staying in the interim CEO role for perhaps longer than Wall Street expects. At the bare minimum, she made the case that Nvidia isn't being led by a group of rookies undeserving of being in the room with a Huang-level exec.
The company's third quarter was solid , the outlook strong, and Kress came across as a steady hand driving the Nvidia rocketship.
For the third quarter, Nvidia posted adjusted earnings of $2.68 a share on revenue of $115.8 billion. Wall Street had expected earnings of $2.47 a share on revenue of $109.15 billion.
Nvidia expects fourth quarter revenue of $127.4 billion to $132.6 billion, comfortably above the $125.25 billion analysts were looking for.
The company said it sees fiscal year 2028 revenue growth of 75%, up from a prior estimate of 70% offered just three months ago.
But pros tell us new Nvidia chair Harvey Jones — who joined Kress on the earnings call — botched the messaging around the timeline of selecting a Huang replacement. Jones lacked a sense of urgency on bringing in a permanent top-notch exec — not what a nervous market wanted to hear from a chip company at the epicenter of the AI boom.
"I don't know that any internal candidate, though, is capable of running the whole company," Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg said on Sozzi Unleashed . "Jensen famously built the structure of the company around himself. Like he's the center of the wheel and all the things connect to him. And I don't think anyone internally has as complete a view of the company as Jensen does."

Prince Harry is forcing himself back into the royal limelight with headline-grabbing antics in a war-torn country, a top royal journalist alleges.
As his popularity continues to wane back home, the Duke of Sussex made a surprise visit Sunday to the Superhuman Center rehabilitation clinic in Lviv, Ukraine, where he fraternized with injured soldiers and assured them they will âwinâ the war with Russia.
âEvery single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth. Youâre going to win the war, and then youâre going to be set up for success,â Harry said at the event.
Harry told Ukrainian soldiers that the United Kingdom has their back.
Efrem Lukatsky/Efrem Lukatsky/via REUTERS
However, former Page Six deputy editor and news commentator Paula Froelich tells The Royalist that she believes the highly publicized trip was another case of Harryâs âattention dependency disorder,â rather than a gesture of actual goodwill.
âIf he doesnât get a headline or heâs not in the paper at least three or four times a week, the poor guy starts to fade away like heâs invisible and doesnât know what to do,â Froelich said. âYou got plenty of veterans at home who need your help, and he ainât paying attention to them.â
Harryâs trip to the east also coincided with Prince William and Princess Catherineâs trip to Mumbai, India, for the Earthshot Prize Awards, a global initiative founded by the next-in-line that awards winners prizes around $1.3 million dollars to bolster environmental solutions.
William and Catherine attended the Earthshot Awards in Mumbai, India on Sunday.
Phil Noble/Phil Noble/REUTERS
âTo put yourself in a position where it looks like you are trying to steal the thunder from an environmental NGOâ¦ just seems so incredibly crass,â The Royalist host Tom Sykes said. âIt just feels like a sort of angry child stamping their feet and going, âLook at me, look at me, look at me,â doesnât it?â
In the public eye, Harryâs friends have maintained that there is no estrangement between him and King Charles. The Sussex couple recently announced that theyâd be staying in England over the holidays, but Sykes suggested it may have something to do with Meghanâs father, Thomas Markle Sr., being arrested in Florida on child pornography charges.
Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, has been arrested on child pornography charges in Florida.
Pinellas County Sheriff's Office/Pinellas County Sheriff's Office/Handout/via REUTERS
âNow theyâre saying theyâre staying here,â Sykes said. âPeople canât help thinking itâs not completely unconnected to developments in Meghanâs family, specifically the orange jumpsuit that her father was photographed wearing the other day.â
In the wake of revelations about her father, Sykes said Meghan has appeared âhauntedâ by her lack of control over the narrative.
âSomething has obviously really massively changed,â Sykes said. âShe looks genuinely like not in control of the situationâ¦ And now weâve got sort of Harry trying to pretend itâs business as usual.â
Froelich said that she was surprised to see such emotional imagery of Meghan, considering she has reportedly known about her fatherâs situation for the last several years.
âSheâs leaning into the role of grief store in chief,â Froelich said. âHeâs leaning into the role of âIâve got your back, soldiers,â when, of course, he only really has his own back.â

articles.title_orig: One of AI's most notorious 'doomers' stands to make billions in Anthropic's IPO
articles.title_zh: One of AI's most notorious 'doomers' stands to make billions in Anthropic's IPO
articles.content_orig:
An Estonian tech billionaire famous for his stance that AI could end humanity is expected to be one of the biggest winners in Anthropic's upcoming IPO .
Jaan Tallinn co-founded Skype and later sold it to eBay . He led Anthropic's first funding round, a $124 million Series A, five years ago — well before the company's Claude chatbot was on the market and took Wall Street and Silicon Valley by storm.
Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT in what could be the largest IPO of all time, and the first public debut for an AI lab.
Tallinn's exact holdings haven't been disclosed. But given Anthropic's expected debut valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion, the return on his initial investment could be well into the tens of billions. His exact return would depend on the level of dilution in subsequent funding rounds and whether he sold any shares along the way.
Anthropic's earliest backers connected with the company through philanthropic circles worried about AI's existential risk. They're sometimes described as "doomers."
In 2020, Tallinn told CNBC that there's a one-in-six chance that humans won't survive this century, referencing a book from Oxford professor Toby Ord. Tallinn also described a runaway AI scenario where a model is left working overnight and "the world is no longer there in the morning."
While he continued to work in tech, Tallinn co-founded the Cambridge Centre for the Study of Existential Risk and the Future of Life Institute , known for one of the first public calls to pause AI. Despite high-profile signatories , including Elon Musk and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak, the institute's "Pause Giant AI Experiments" letter in 2023 had little effect on the industry.
Tallinn's view on AI was influenced by researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky, who co-authored the 2025 book "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies," about the catastrophic risk of AI without proper checks, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Tallinn, who has an estimated net worth of omore than $10 billion, later crossed paths with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who had defected from OpenAI with his eventual co-founders, citing views that Sam Altman's company wasn't taking AI safety seriously enough.
Amodei and Tallinn overlapped in the effective altruism community, according to people who know both of them. Effective altruism, sometimes known as EA , is a philosophy that aims to use data and evidence to maximize philanthropic impact. While there's no official membership, its Silicon Valley network ended up generating much of Anthropic's early venture capital money, according to multiple people.
Tallinn's early bet was that bankrolling a safety-conscious AI company was one of the best ways to keep a lid on the risk, these people said. Tallinn also invested in DeepMind, which was later acquired by Google .
One person, who asked not to be named, said that at the time of Tallinn's investment, there was no expectation that Anthropic "would be a profitable undertaking." Venture investors hadn't yet gone all-in on AI, and it was "before the era of putting AI in your pitch deck," said the person, who asked not to be named in order to speak candidly on the matter.
Tallinn declined to be interviewed for this story.
Anthropic's first round in 2021 also included Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, who founded Open Philanthropy — now known as Coefficient Giving — which is deeply rooted in effective altruism. The charity was co-founded by Holden Karnofsky, husband of Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei. Karnofsky also started GiveWell, also largely tied to effective altruism.
Former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried, another known effective altruist, backed Anthropic in its early days alongside Tallinn. Bankman-Fried participated in the Series B in 2022 through his now-defunct hedge fund Alameda Research. The former CEO was convicted of fraud in 2023 and sentenced to 25 years in prison. His stake was sold in bankruptcy auction at a fraction of the company's current valuation.
Tallinn's early investment initially put Anthropic's price tag at $461 million, according to Pitchbook. It has ballooned in value since, and last raised money at a $965 billion valuation in private markets. The lab has raised money from tech giants Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia, and plans to sell $26 billion worth of shares to a group of tech companies at the IPO price.
Anthropic's early investors and some in the safety community aren't overwhelmingly cheering the IPO. Many worry behind the scenes that AI safety will take a backseat to Anthropic's commercial success and wider shareholder base, according to a person close to the group.
Many in the AI safety community "are opposed to the IPO," this person said.
Others point to Anthropic's unique corporate structure that gives the founders broad discretion and control of the company through a single super-voting share. The co-founders will be sole members of "Founder LLC," which will hold 50.1% of the voting power. But Anthropic is also built as a public benefit corporation, meaning it has a dual mandate beyond just a duty to shareholders. It has to serve the best interests of its "company purpose" to facilitate the "responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."

articles.title_orig: Israeli tanks roll into central Gaza in first ground operation since ceasefire began
articles.title_zh: Israeli tanks roll into central Gaza in first ground operation since ceasefire began
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of displaced Palestinians fled their tents and shelters in central ‌Gaza on Wednesday as Israeli tanks advanced, in what the Israeli military said was an operation targeting Hamas infrastructure outside areas that Israel controls in ⁠the enclave.
Witnesses said some Israeli tanks rolled onto the main Salahudeen road, west of the Yellow Line that marks the boundary of the two-thirds of the Gaza Strip still under Israeli control despite ⁠a ceasefire that has ​lasted more ⁠than a year.
An Israeli airstrike near the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
The medics ⁠said separate Israeli airstrikes had killed two other people ​earlier ⁠in the day in ‌ Deir al-Balah and Gaza City.
An Israeli military spokesperson told NBC News that the military was carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of ‌the Yellow Line in central Gaza ‌and that it had struck a militant in southern Gaza earlier on Wednesday.
They later confirmed that it was the first ground operation since the U.S. brokered ceasefire came into effect in October 2025 .
Dozens of Palestinians, most of whom have been displaced multiple times since the start of the war in 2023, piled their belongings on top of bicycles, wheelchairs, motorcycles and vehicles as ​they fled the area.
Salam Aql said the military had ordered residents of the area to leave “but we wanted to stay because we ​are exhausted from being displaced so many times.”
“We are tired, I swear to God, we are tired. But as we were sitting there, gunfire started ‌coming ⁠in,” she said, adding that a boy was hit in the leg by a bullet.
“Once he was wounded, we could not stay any longer.”
Hamas said the Israeli military’s raid and forced displacement of Palestinians marked a ceasefire violation and a ​dangerous escalation.
The truce halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war, although it has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas’ disarmament.
The Israeli military spokesperson had no immediate comment on other strikes.
Residents reported hearing tank shells being fired in the area. An Israeli airstrike near the location of the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
Israel, which says Hamas has recently been regrouping and rearming, has stepped up attacks against the Islamist group. Hamas has accused Israel of attempting to derail the U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement.
Gaza health ‌authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been ​killed since the ceasefire went into effect, while ‌the Israeli military says five Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Palestinian authorities say more ⁠than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the military campaign ‌that Israel ​launched there after Hamas-led fighters killed ‌about 1,200 people in southern ​Israel in an attack on October 7, 2023.
The body overseeing US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the Gaza war on Wednesday ​accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments to end hostilities, leaving the population of Gaza in dire conditions and the ‌ceasefire in danger of collapse.
The 12-page Board of Peace report, seen by Reuters, is the body’s second to the United Nations Security Council since the US-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a sobering assessment of progress made since then.
The board, established and headed by Trump, is expected to present the report’s findings to a meeting of the council in New York at ​the end of November.
“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” ​the report said, warning that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.”
While the ceasefire has halted major ⁠fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect ​last year.
Hamas agreed in July to a Board of Peace roadmap to surrender its weapons and transfer governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority, but Israel rejected the ​roadmap, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas is dismantled.
Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza, while the report said Hamas fighters have also continued attacks on Israeli troops.
“Every day that Israel continues strikes against Hamas targets, it delays putting Hamas’ agreement to the roadmap to the test,” the report said.
“Meanwhile, Hamas militant activity continues, the commitment to cease all military activities has not ​been met in full by the parties, and the population faces another winter in tents and rubble.”
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim dismissed the report as “pure disinformation”, accusing the ​Board of Peace of providing cover to Israel to evade its commitments under the plan to end the war and to continue its aggression in Gaza.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister ‌Benjamin Netanyahu ⁠and a spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: 10-Year-Old NGINX HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code on Servers
articles.title_zh: 10-Year-Old NGINX HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code on Servers
articles.content_orig:
A flaw in NGINX 's HTTP/2 support can allow an attacker to run code on servers with HTTP/2 enabled, without needing to log in.
The decade-old flaw, CVE-2026-123007, dubbed " nginx2root ," has been present in NGINX's open-source code since version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015. Fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 came out today.
F5 , the company behind NGINX, says attackers can run code where ASLR is turned off or can be bypassed. Security researchers at Wiz said they bypassed ASLR and ran code through the flaw in tests. Xint's researchers said they ran code through it with nothing more than a reachable HTTP/2 port.
Code run this way gets the permissions of an NGINX worker process. Getting root on the host takes a second way to raise privileges, according to CIRCL, the Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg.
In Xint's tests, code running as a worker could get root on the host through a separate bug in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, even when NGINX ran inside a Docker container.
Neither the vendor nor the Wiz and Rapid7 researchers have reported any attacks exploiting the flaw so far. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog did not list it as of today.
Proof-of-concept code for the flaw is publicly available on GitHub, but its notes state it is suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started Docker container on the same machine.
Every open-source release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is vulnerable, according to NGINX's security advisories . That includes 1.31.8 from October 21, as well as the October 14 security releases 1.31.7 and 1.30.6.
NGINX Plus is affected too, in 37.x releases before the fixed builds and in R34 to R36, according to the vendor advisory .
Today's releases also fix four more flaws that the vendor says can lead to code execution under the same ASLR condition. It scores all five 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0.
Each flaw can be reached only in a particular setup:
HTTP/2 is on where a listen directive includes http2 , or where http2 on is set. Running openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against a server shows whether it accepts HTTP/2: the output reads ALPN protocol: h2 if it does. Behind a CDN, test the NGINX origin itself, because an origin that accepts only HTTP/1.1 cannot be attacked through HTTP/2.
These releases fix CVE-2026-123007, according to F5:
Versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix all five flaws, according to NGINX's release notes . On NGINX Plus, 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 fix four of the flaws, and the CVE-2026-123633 fix was introduced in the earlier builds 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1.
After upgrading, restart NGINX fully or use its live binary upgrade. A reload alone leaves the old executable running, and existing connections can stay on old worker processes.
The official Docker images for NGINX had 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 tags as of today, including Alpine variants.
Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages as of today. Ubuntu's CVE status page listed nginx as vulnerable on its releases from 16.04 to 26.10, and Debian's security tracker listed it as vulnerable in bookworm, trixie, forky and sid. A distribution package can carry a fix without changing the version number that nginx -v reports, so compare the full package version with the distribution's own advisory.
The vendor lists workarounds for only two of the five flaws. For the resolver flaw, CVE-2026-123634, avoid SSI and mirror directives, and do not build a proxied server name from variables. For the mail proxy flaw, CVE-2026-113425, limit listeners to trusted networks.
CIRCL's response guidance lists turning off HTTP/2 as a temporary mitigation until you can upgrade. That blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, but not the other three flaws. Turning off HTTP/3 where it is used removes the setup that CVE-2026-121810 needs.
On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in each affected server block and remove http2 from its listen directives. On 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove http2 from the listen directive, so listen 443 ssl http2; becomes listen 443 ssl; . Then restart NGINX where needed and rerun the openssl check to confirm the server no longer accepts HTTP/2.
Until the Linux kernel's SCTP bug is fixed, the same guidance advises that hosts not using SCTP, a network transport protocol like TCP, block its kernel module from loading. One way is to add the line install sctp /bin/false to a .conf file in /etc/modprobe.d/ . That does not unload a module already loaded or turn off SCTP built into the kernel.
For signs of an attack, CIRCL suggests looking for NGINX workers that start unexpected programs, workers that exit abnormally or leave core dumps, long-lived HTTP/2 connections with heavy incoming traffic but few logged requests, and unusual outbound connections or DNS lookups. A clean access log does not rule out an attack, because HTTP/2 control frames do not normally show up there as requests. None of these signs is proof on its own.
Rapid7's version of the attack needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, according to its technical analysis . The attack took two and a half minutes in its demonstration. On links slower than about 300 Mbit/s, the transfer would run past NGINX's default one-hour connection limit, and the attack would fail.
The method also depends on a glibc memory-copy routine that is chosen on x86-64 CPUs with the avx512f and avx512vl features.
Wiz ran its tests on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds, using HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems, according to its disclosure post .
Xint's attack worked against its test servers on AWS, GCP and Azure, including over a public IP address, according to its research report .
